result:
There is a specific kind of magic that only happens in a city when it rains at night. The asphalt turns into a dark mirror, fracturing the neon reds of taillights and the harsh whites of streetlamps into long, impressionistic streaks. People hurry past, hunched beneath the dark domes of their umbrellas, entirely focused on the puddle directly in front of their shoes. 

Standing under the awning of a closed bakery, you can experience a sudden, overwhelming sense of *sonder*. That woman in the yellow coat running for the bus—she has a favorite childhood memory, a secret fear she never tells anyone, and a song currently stuck in her head. The man walking his reluctant terrier has a whole history of heartbreaks and triumphs that have led him to this exact, soggy crosswalk. We are all protagonists in epics that simply overlap in the background of everyone else’s chapters. 

We spend so much of our lives trapped inside the loud, echoing chambers of our own minds, convinced that our anxieties and ambitions are the center of the universe. Yet, there is a profound relief in realizing how small we actually are. The rain doesn't care about the email you forgot to send or the awkward thing you said three years ago. It just falls, washing the dust off the leaves and the pavement alike. When you finally step out from under the awning, you aren't the main character anymore; you are just another drop of water returning to the ocean.
